teaser.en: Unlike most seagrasses, it grows woody stems that rise from the seabed, carrying fans of curved leaves like little underwater palms.

summary.en: Sickle-leaved seagrass is one of the two most common seagrasses in Kenya, forming dense meadows on the sandy and rocky floors of the lagoons. Its meadows shelter the fish and octopus that coastal fishers rely on.

about.en:
Sickle-leaved seagrass is a flowering plant that lives fully submerged in the sea. It is sturdier than most seagrasses: tough, woody stems rise from the seabed, each topped with a fan of flat, curved leaves shaped like a sickle. A meadow of it looks like a tiny underwater forest of palms.

Its strong roots and creeping rhizomes can grip rock as well as sand, so it can grow where other seagrasses cannot.

where.en: It forms dense meadows on sandy and rocky lagoon bottoms and is one of the two predominant seagrasses on the Kenyan coast. Seagrass meadows fringe Gazi Bay, Diani-Chale and Vanga-Shimoni. It usually stays under water, so snorkellers in the lagoons see it best.

uses.en: Its meadows are habitat for the rabbitfish, parrotfish, octopus and sea cucumbers that Digo fishers depend on. They also trap sediment and help to protect beaches.

names.en: No Digo name has been recorded yet. Swahili speakers usually call sea plants in general *mwani*. In English it is sickle-leaved seagrass, and its scientific name is *Thalassodendron ciliatum*, which means 'sea tree'.

conservation.en: The seagrass meadows of Gazi Bay, Diani-Chale and Vanga-Shimoni are feeding grounds for dugongs, green turtles and rabbitfish, and nurseries for young fish.
